title: Building a Configuration System
subtopics: Failing safely when configuration is invalid
learning_outcomes: Describe Centralized configuration and explain how it relates to Building a Configuration System.
Demonstrate Configuration validation in a small Node.js example and predict the observable result.
Test a failure, boundary, lifecycle, or version-compatibility case involving Required and optional values.

content.intro: Building a Configuration System is part of process configuration and environment. This lesson connects Centralized configuration, Configuration validation, Required and optional values to a concrete Node.js example. Focus on the behavior you can observe, the assumptions the API makes, and one failure or boundary case.
content.why_it_matters: The process object exposes runtime state, command-line input, environment configuration, signals, and shutdown behavior. Test missing, invalid, and valid environment values in separate runs without placing secrets in source code.

content_blocks.title: The core idea
content_blocks.text: The process object exposes runtime state, command-line input, environment configuration, signals, and shutdown behavior. Validate configuration at startup and fail clearly when required settings are missing or malformed.

items.title: Centralized configuration
items.text: Treat environment values as untrusted strings: parse them, validate required settings at startup, and never print secrets in logs.

items.title: Failing safely when configuration is invalid
items.text: Treat environment values as untrusted strings: parse them, validate required settings at startup, and never print secrets in logs.

content_blocks.code:
function parsePort(value = '3000') { const port = Number(value); if (!Number.isInteger(port) || port < 1 || port > 65535) throw new Error('Invalid port'); return port; }
console.log(parsePort('8080'));
content_blocks.run_instructions: Inspect this JavaScript in a local Node.js project. It is a static-validation teaching example: CodeLeaf does not run this arbitrary example in the API process. If it needs a package, file, server, database, or external service, provision that dependency in a separate local project and follow its official setup instructions. Run with `node example.mjs` when the example is self-contained, or adapt the required imports/inputs first.
content_blocks.reset_steps: Restore the starting snippet and inputs. Repeat with one different valid value and one invalid, missing, empty, or failure input appropriate to the example.

content_blocks.title: Guided example
content_blocks.text: Start with the code shown above. Predict the result before running it, then verify it against: 3000 when PORT is unset; otherwise the validated configured port. Change one input or simulate one failure and describe how the behavior should change. Test missing, invalid, and valid environment values in separate runs without placing secrets in source code.

content_blocks.title: Runtime and safety note
content_blocks.text: Teaching baseline: use a supported Node.js LTS release (Node.js 24 LTS as checked on 2026-10-13). The official releases page lists Node.js 26 as Current and Node.js 24/22 as LTS. Some advanced APIs, flags, permission behavior, embedded SQLite capabilities, module-loader hooks, and TypeScript integration are version-sensitive; verify the exact installed runtime. The Node.js 22 runtime available in the build-check environment is used only for syntax checks. This example is for learning and static validation, not for executing untrusted learner code inside CodeLeaf.

content.task: Create or inspect a small Node.js example for Building a Configuration System. Include at least one listed subtopic, document the expected result, and verify a normal case plus a boundary or failure case.
task_acceptance_criteria: The example demonstrates a named lesson concept, rather than only mentioning the title.
Expected output or observable behavior is documented and reproducible.
At least one invalid, empty, timeout, resource, or failure case is handled or explained.
The solution does not put secrets in source code and does not execute untrusted code inside the production API process.
hints: Start with Centralized configuration; identify the input, operation, and observable result.
Run the smallest relevant example in the selected Node.js release before adding frameworks or external services.
Test one failure or boundary case for Configuration validation, then explain why the outcome is expected.

common_mistakes.problem: Assuming environment values are already validated or doing asynchronous work after the process exit event.
common_mistakes.why: The code may pass a simple demonstration yet fail with real inputs, resource limits, timing, or runtime differences.
common_mistakes.fix: Parse configuration once, validate its shape, and use a deliberate graceful-shutdown sequence.

common_mistakes.problem: Copying a snippet without checking its runtime, dependencies, input assumptions, or cleanup behavior.
common_mistakes.why: Node.js APIs and surrounding ecosystem tools have explicit version, trust, and resource boundaries.
common_mistakes.fix: State the environment and dependency assumptions, then rerun the example from a clean starting state.
